paragraphs.text: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-89 (DEE89) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by loss of function of GAD67, the enzyme that converts glutamic acid to GABA. Seizures begin in the neonatal period or early infancy, often as epileptic spasms or myoclonic seizures, with suppression-burst or hypsarrhythmia on EEG. Affected children have severe to profound developmental delay and abnormal muscle tone. Some patients also have cleft palate, joint contractures or pes equinovarus, omphalocele, scoliosis or dysmorphic facial features (Chatron et al., 2020; Neuray et al., 2020).

checks.claim: DEE89 is an autosomal recessive disorder.
checks.evidence_quote: In all families, Sanger sequencing confirmed segregation of the GAD1 variants with the disease phenotype (Supplementary Fig. 1) and a recessive mode of inheritance associated with the disease.

paragraphs.text: Chatron et al. (2020) reported 11 patients from 6 unrelated families of Algerian, Egyptian, Turkish (2 families), Iranian and Brazilian origin. All patients were born to consanguineous parents who were first or second cousins. Seizures began in the first 2 months of life in all patients. In the 10 patients whose early disease history was available, onset was in the first month, mainly as epileptic spasms or myoclonic seizures. EEG at onset showed a suppression-burst pattern or a variant with interburst attenuation in 7 of 8 patients recorded in the neonatal period. The 2 patients first recorded later had hypsarrhythmia. Antiepileptic drugs eventually controlled seizures in 6 patients, and in 5 of these, seizures were controlled for long periods after vigabatrin was added. All living patients had severe psychomotor delay, and intellectual disability was profound in every patient who could be assessed. Head circumference was normal in all but 1 patient. Brain MRI was normal in 5 patients. Abnormal findings in other patients included a hypoplastic corpus callosum with dilated subarachnoid spaces in 1 patient and mild cerebral atrophy with ventricular enlargement at 6 years in another. Seven patients had cleft palate, 6 had joint contractures, 5 had pes equinovarus and 4 had scoliosis. Three patients had dysmorphic facial features with no clear common elements. Chatron et al. (2020) considered markedly increased muscle tone to be a core feature seen in all patients, although axial hypotonia was also frequent. Four patients had died before 4 years of age.

paragraphs.text: Within the cohort of Chatron et al. (2020), the 2 affected sibs of Egyptian Family B both had omphalocele, pes equinovarus, arthrogryposis and multiple dysmorphic features, and both had seizures from 2 weeks of age. The sister also had cleft soft palate, jejunal atresia, a branchial fistula, multiple hemangiomas, camptodactyly, scoliosis and abnormal external genitalia. She died at 2 years of age of failure to thrive and respiratory infection. Her brother died at 4 years of age. In Turkish Family E, the proband had facial dysmorphism, cleft palate, Hirschsprung disease, pes equinovarus, flexion contractures, cervical and axillary webbing, and epileptic spasms with hypsarrhythmia. His older brother was born at 29 weeks' gestation with cleft palate, myoclonic seizures, congenital heart disease and pes equinovarus, and died of sepsis on postnatal day 9. In Turkish Family C, both sibs had refractory epilepsy from the neonatal period and cleft palate. The brother died of refractory seizures at 2 years of age, after his seizures worsened on a ketogenic diet.

paragraphs.text: Neuray et al. (2020) reported 6 patients from 6 unrelated families of Persian, Pakistani, African American, Sudanese, Egyptian and Turkish ancestry. The text stated that 4 patients were born to consanguineous parents, but the clinical table listed parental consanguinity in 5 families. All patients were born at term after a normal pregnancy. Seizures began between 2 and 6 months of age and were mainly focal motor seizures with or without impaired awareness. Two patients also had epileptic spasms, 4 had focal non-motor seizures and 5 had bilateral motor seizures. Seizures were controlled with medication in 3 patients and were drug-resistant in the other 3. EEG at onset showed burst suppression in 2 patients, diffuse slowing with multifocal and generalized sharp waves in 2, and hypsarrhythmia in 2. Cranial MRI was normal in all but 2 patients, 1 with slight ventricular enlargement and 1 with moderate global atrophy. All patients had severe developmental delay. Most achieved no speech, and only 1 developed simple speech. Five of the 6 had reduced muscle strength, 4 had slight dysmorphic facial features, and only 1 had cleft palate. Other features without clear common elements included hirsutism, kidney stones, urogenital malformations, diastasis recti, reduced head circumference, clinodactyly, short arms, arthrogryposis of the lower limbs and congenital hip dislocation. Metabolic workups were normal. Neuray et al. (2020) noted that all patients still had severe intellectual disability despite seizure freedom in 3 of them.

paragraphs.text: Chatron et al. (2020) studied 11 patients with DEE89 from 6 consanguineous families, ascertained through GeneMatcher. Using whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing, they identified homozygous GAD1 mutations in all affected individuals. Four families carried mutations predicted to truncate the protein: a splice site mutation (c.1414-1G-C) in Family A, a 5-bp deletion (c.812_816delTTAAG) in Family C, and a nonsense mutation (R531X) shared by Families D and E. Family B carried an in-frame 3-bp deletion (c.695_697delAGA; K232del), and Family F carried a missense mutation (E509K). Sanger sequencing confirmed segregation in all families. In Family A, cDNA analysis found no normal mRNA product and showed 3 aberrant transcripts. In a cell-free expression system, the K232del protein was expressed at levels comparable to wild type, so loss of function could not be formally demonstrated for this variant.
